title: HS2 reset, costs and Euston—what’s changed and what still worries MPs
label: 14 September 2026 · Delivering HS2 & Euston
summary: The Department for Transport and HS2 Ltd told MPs how they’ve tried to stabilise the troubled HS2 project after big cost increases and delays. Witnesses described a reset of the programme, technical changes to reduce risk, ongoing contract renegotiations with major builders, plans for the Euston station area and how surplus land will be handled. They stressed there’s still substantial uncertainty about final costs and timing and that stronger governance and clearer baselines are being put in place.

chapters.title: Why HS2 needed a 'reset'
chapters.takeaway: MPs were told HS2 had big coordination and design problems, so the company and Department ran a reset to get a reliable plan.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The programme has ballooned in cost and slipped in schedule. Could you introduce yourselves and tell us what's changed since 2024?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: I'm Jo Shanmugalingam, the Department's top civil servant. The National Audit Office—an independent public spending watchdog—said HS2 'has not gone as planned'. We're accountable for that and have backed a thorough reset to get cost and schedule under control.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: I'm Mark Wild, HS2's CEO. In 2024 the programme lacked a clear, reliable plan, designs weren't mature and contracts left most risk with HS2. We ran a five-step reset to find root causes and to put things back in sequence.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: I'm Dean Creamer, the Department's senior lead for major rail projects. Part of my job is to act as the programme sponsor and make sure the reset is joined up with Government oversight and commercial advice.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We looked at what went wrong: starting work too early with incomplete design, contracts that pushed risk onto HS2, and weak programme control. The reset fixed sequencing, found missing scope, and produced what we call the 'reference case'—a realistic plan for delivery.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You used the term 'reference case'. What's that in plain English?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: It’s the practical version of the programme we think we can deliver: forward-leaning but built on things we can actually achieve, unlike the over-optimistic plans from earlier phases.

chapters.title: Costs, ranges and the new baseline
chapters.takeaway: They've published wide cost and schedule ranges, are building a new detailed baseline to measure progress, but uncertainty still remains.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You now say completion could cost between £87.7bn and £102.7bn, and full services might not start until 2040–43. How can we be sure that won’t rise further?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We accept past failings. The NAO praised the reset work but warned not to rush exiting it. We're making sure the Department and HS2 have a stronger grip before we lock in the new plan.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We're forming 'baseline 8.0'—think of a baseline as the detailed schedule and budget we'll report against. If it isn't robust we'll keep working. It should be ready by Christmas, and if not we'll aim for April. That baseline will give MPs a clear line of sight into delivery.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: There will always be uncertainty: over 10 years remain and many risks can pop up. The ranges are meant to cover foreseeable uncertainties, but not extreme 'black swan' events like wars or hyperinflation.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: If there's still big uncertainty, doesn't that leave a huge envelope where costs can climb? How confident can you be?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The ranges deliberately acknowledge uncertainty. I'm tasked with driving the programme to the lower end of the range and the contracts and incentives are being used to push everyone in that direction.

chapters.title: Technical choices to reduce risk
chapters.takeaway: They've cut top speed and dropped automatic train operation to make testing and commissioning simpler and safer.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: You reduced train speed to 300 kph and removed automatic train driving. Will that really lower cost and risk, and do passengers lose out?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Ministers asked for options that keep safety and benefits and get service running sooner and cheaper. The advice was that reducing technical novelty reduces testing time and cost.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Lowering speed to about 300 kph uses the same proven tech anyone building high-speed rail in France or Spain would use, so testing is far simpler. And we removed 'automatic train operation'—where computers drive the train for you—because the necessary high-speed version doesn't exist in the real world at the level we'd need.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Passengers lose only a few minutes—London to Birmingham becomes three minutes longer—but we get a big drop in technical risk and a better chance to open earlier at good quality.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: This trade-off is about derisking commissioning. The department thinks the benefits-cost ratio won't be materially harmed but the programme is easier to deliver.

chapters.title: Contracts, renegotiation and cancellation numbers
chapters.takeaway: Early contract choices left HS2 carrying too much risk; some deals have been reset to add incentives, but renegotiations and any cancellation costs remain uncertain.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Why were the original contracts—NEC3-style, cost-reimbursable arrangements—used? They seem to have left HS2 'hostage' to contractors.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: NEC3 is a standard contract form (it's a common construction contract) but the real problem was starting with immature designs and asking suppliers to fix prices. Contractors couldn't carry that risk, so the risk flowed back to HS2 and became cost-reimbursable.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Are your renegotiations real savings or just potential savings? How much of that £2bn upside is at risk?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: With two big civils contractors—EKFB and Align—we've settled the past on public money principles, fixed fees for future work and added incentives for early delivery. That reintroduces commercial tension and makes savings more real, but it's not a cure-all and uncertainty persists on the remaining main civils contracts.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We must be prepared in case some deals don’t get done; HS2 needs contingency plans so the programme can keep moving.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: About the cost of cancelling the project: the Department used a method and applied a large 'optimism bias'—66% from the Treasury Green Book guidance. That looks subjective. Will you get independent verification of your cancellation-cost work?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: I was asked to verify methodology. Given we lack exact designs for putting things back, using a percentage of what’s been spent to estimate remediation is a reasonable approach. The 66% is the top end of Green Book guidance for immaturity and felt prudent.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We chose a proportionate approach so the HS2 team could focus on delivery. But we will consider the Committee’s recommendation on independent verification and discuss it with Ministers.

chapters.title: Euston station, governance and community impacts
chapters.takeaway: Euston is being handled through an Euston Delivery Company with partners to get joined-up planning, but costs and funding routes still need detailed design and time.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Euston has four big pieces—new HS2 station, the existing station, local transport and property development. Is the current £8bn estimate mature?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: No. Costs at Euston are less mature than phase 1. We've set up an Euston Delivery Company (EDC) to be the 'guiding mind'—one place to align HS2, Network Rail, Transport for London and local government.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: EDC will oversee time, cost and benefits, bring partners into the tent, get a spatial plan and then move into concept design. Only once partners’ requirements and a concept are agreed will we refine the funding ask.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Is the EDC fully staffed?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: About 30 posts exist now. We're appointing a chief executive who will become its accounting officer, and we'll scale capability with secondments from partner bodies. We expect a fuller plan to be signed off next year before big spending.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Local people near Euston have been badly affected. Who’s making sure walking routes, tube connections, buses, taxis and drop-offs are designed in from the start?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: That's a core EDC task. TfL, Network Rail and HS2 sit on the EDC board so operational needs—like bus interchanges or safe walking links—are considered in the concept design before decisions are signed off.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We’re also working to reduce disruption—moving spoil by rail instead of lorry, opening skills and community hubs, and funding local mitigation—but communities like Drummond Street have suffered and need continued focus.

chapters.title: Surplus land and property returns
chapters.takeaway: The Department is preparing to dispose of properties bought for cancelled parts of HS2, but will move carefully to protect local markets and taxpayers.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: You bought lots of land and houses. Why has returning unused land taken so long, and what’s the plan now?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: There are different groups of land. On the eastern/Leeds leg we have about 500 properties no longer needed; 300 of those qualify for the Crichel Down rule (giving original owners a right to be offered land back). We’ve appointed an agent and expect a disposal strategy by October, with some sales or rentals starting this year.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Isn’t delaying sales risky—markets fall and empty land can harm communities?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We must balance speed with getting good value and avoid flooding local markets. Temporary possessions and remediation work are already under way; some temporary land works (filling boreholes etc.) will finish in the next 18 months.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Where possible we'll rent properties to avoid waste, maintain listed buildings appropriately, and dispose of land in a managed way. Ministers and I monitor this closely.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Will you commit to independent checks on cancellation-cost estimates and disposal plans?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We’ll consider the Committee’s recommendation about independent verification. Our current approach was chosen as proportionate so HS2 could focus on delivery, but we’ll keep options under review.

Members of Parliament — elected representatives who sit in the House of Commons and hold the Government to account.
Refers to NEC3, a standard form of construction contract used in the UK to allocate risk and manage building works.
A contract type where the client pays a contractor’s allowable costs plus a fee, rather than a fixed total price.
Construction firms specialising in civil engineering works like earthworks, tunnels, bridges and large infrastructure.
The name of one of the major civil‑engineering contractor consortia working on HS2.

HM Treasury’s official guidance on appraising and evaluating public projects and spending decisions.
A built‑in allowance in project estimates to guard against the common tendency to underestimate costs and timescales.
A UK rule giving previous landowners a right to be offered government surplus land back before it is sold more widely.
A coordinating body set up to align HS2, Network Rail, TfL and local government on the Euston redevelopment.
The public body that owns, manages and maintains most of Britain’s railway infrastructure.
The local government body responsible for most transport services across Greater London (Tube, buses, trams, etc.).
A senior official personally accountable to Parliament for the regularity and propriety of how public funds are spent in their organisation.
Temporary loaning of staff from one organisation to work in another for a set period.
Soil, rock and other material excavated and removed from a construction site.
Legal temporary rights to use land for construction works without permanently buying it.
The rules and expectations that taxpayer funds are used properly, transparently and to achieve best value.
Calculations of how much it would cost to stop and dismantle a project, including remediation, compensation and other closures.
